questions.text: Consider product of three matrices [latex]M_{1}[/latex],[latex]M_{2}[/latex] and [latex]M_{3}[/latex] having w rows and x columns, x rows and y columns, and y rows and z columns. Under what condition will it take less time to compute the product as [latex]\left(M_{1} M_{2}\right) M_{3}[/latex] than to compute [latex]M_{1}\left(M_{2} M_{3}\right)[/latex] ?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- [latex](M_1M_2)M_3[/latex]: [latex]wxy+wyz[/latex] multiplications.
- [latex]M_1(M_2M_3)[/latex]: [latex]xyz+wxz[/latex] multiplications.

First is cheaper when [latex]wxy+wyz \lt xyz+wxz[/latex]. Divide by wxyz: [latex]\frac1z+\frac1x \lt \frac1w+\frac1y[/latex].

Answer: (1/x + 1/z) [latex]\lt[/latex] (1/w + 1/y)

questions.text: Of the following sort algorithms, which has execution time that is least dependant on initial ordering of the input?
questions.solution:
Merge sort always splits in half and merges, so it takes [latex]\Theta(n\log n)[/latex] for every input order. Insertion sort ([latex]n[/latex] to [latex]n^2[/latex]) and quick sort ([latex]n\log n[/latex] to [latex]n^2[/latex]) depend heavily on the initial order.

Answer: Merge sort

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

The outer loop runs [latex]\log_2 n[/latex] times (i doubles) and the inner loop n times [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]\Theta(n\log n)[/latex].

[latex]O(n^2)[/latex], [latex]O(n\log n)[/latex] and [latex]O(n\log n\log n)[/latex] are valid upper bounds, but [latex]O(n)[/latex] is too small, so it is not a valid bound.

(This question was excluded from ISRO's evaluation because of its unclear wording.)

Answer: O(n)

questions.text: Huffman tree is constructed for the following data :{A,B,C,D,E} with frequency {0.17, 0.11, 0.24, 0.33 and 0.15} respectively. 100 00 01101 is decoded as
questions.solution:
Huffman merges: B (0.11) + E (0.15) = 0.26; A (0.17) + C (0.24) = 0.41; 0.26 + D (0.33) = 0.59; 0.41 + 0.59 = 1.
With 0 for the smaller (left) branch: A = 00, C = 01, B = 100, E = 101, D = 11.

Decode 1000001101: 100 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] B, 00 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] A, 01 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] C, 101 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] E.

Answer: BACE

questions.text: G  is an undirected graph with vertex set {v1, v2, v3, v4, v5, v6, v7} and edge set {v1v2, v1v3, v1v4 ,v2v4, v2v5, v3v4, v4v5, v4v6, v5v6, v6v7 }. A breadth first search of the graph is performed with v1 as the root node. Which of the following is a tree edge?
questions.solution:
BFS from v1 first visits all neighbours of v1: v2, v3, v4. So v1v2, v1v3 and v1v4 are tree edges.
v2v4, v3v4 join two vertices already at level 1, and v4v5 is not used if v5 is first discovered from v2.

Answer: v1v4
